due.line: I. J. Good judged it more likely than not that a machine surpassing every human intellect would be built within the twentieth century, setting off an intelligence explosion.

Ray Solomonoff expected a general theory of AI most likely within two to twenty-five years, and a machine with human-level problem-solving in its designed fields perhaps as little as a decade or so later.
Ray Kurzweil projected that around 2023 a thousand dollars of computer hardware would buy raw processing equal to his own estimate for one human brain.
The AI 2027 scenario forecast that during 2025 AI company revenues would triple, yearly data-centre spending would double, and US AI power draw would grow by over five gigawatts.
The AI 2027 scenario had AI assistants speeding the leading lab's algorithmic progress by about half again by early 2026.

fiction.author: Rudy Rucker

intro: People have been dating the arrival of machines smarter than us since the 1960s. This page puts their calls on one line, from the mathematicians who first imagined an intelligence explosion to this summer's revised timelines, and reads each against what this site measures tonight. Nobody on it is crowned: the page shows who said what, when they said it, what would prove them wrong, and which way the evidence leans so far.

lanes.definition: An AI system a lab would rather use than its best human engineers for writing and fixing software.

forecasts.line: Ajeya Cotra's median for the longest METR fifty-percent time horizon reported by the end of 2026 was about twenty-four hours of expert work.
All model-based forecasts have 2027 as one of the most likely years that SC being developed, which is when an SC arrives in the AI 2027 scenario.
According to a recent METR report, the length of coding tasks AIs can handle, their “time horizon”, doubled every 7 months from 2019 - 2024 and every 4 months from 2024-onward.
forecasts.who: AI Futures Project (Kokotajlo, Lifland, Jurkovic et al.)

forecasts.line: Daniel Kokotajlo's August 2026 median for an automated coder, an AI that labs would rather keep than their human coders, is November 2027.
Eli Lifland's August 2026 median for an automated coder, an AI that labs would rather keep than their human coders, is January 2030.

lanes.label: A machine that out-codes the best programmers

lanes.definition: A system that can carry out the work of an AI research team, so each model helps build the next.

forecasts.line: The AI 2027 scenario had AI assistants speeding the leading lab's algorithmic progress by about half again by early 2026.
Sam Altman wrote that 2026 would likely bring AI systems able to work out genuinely new insights.
Leopold Aschenbrenner called it strikingly plausible that models could do the job of the engineers and researchers who build AI by 2027.
The AI 2027 scenario placed a superhuman AI researcher, one that outdoes the best people at AI research, at around September 2027.
We are making strong progress toward creating an automated AI researcher by March of 2028.
William MacAskill and Fin Moorhouse think it fairly likely that AI matches human research labour within two decades, and possibly well within one.

lanes.label: AI that does AI research

undated.line: Ajeya Cotra gave about one chance in ten that AI fully automates AI research and development, matching human researchers, by the end of 2026.

lanes.definition: AI that matches people at almost all cognitive work, or does enough of it to transform the economy the way the industrial revolution did.

forecasts.line: Ray Solomonoff expected a general theory of AI most likely within two to twenty-five years, and a machine with human-level problem-solving in its designed fields perhaps as little as a decade or so later.
Sam Altman told TIME that OpenAI would have an internal system he would call AGI before the end of 2026, while conceding it was not there yet.
The AI 2027 scenario expects AI to be doing a quarter of the remote jobs of 2024 by October 2027, with unemployment about a point higher than a year before.
Mustafa Suleyman predicted an AI could turn a modest stake into a million dollars selling online, with light human help within a year and probably entirely on its own within three to five years.
Leopold Aschenbrenner expects that in 2027 or 2028 models will be as capable as the leading experts and work much like a drop-in remote employee.
If these scaling laws continue for only a year or two longer, we are likely to get what I’ve called Powerful AI, or “a country of geniuses in a datacenter”.
Daniel Kokotajlo's August 2026 median for AI that matches or exceeds the best human experts on almost every cognitive task is November 2028.
Ray Kurzweil bet publicly that a machine would pass a rigorous Turing test, judged under formal rules with expert interrogators, by 2029.
Demis Hassabis expects AGI around 2030, give or take a year, and says that looking back people will see we are already on the lower slopes of the singularity.
Eli Lifland's August 2026 median for AI that matches or exceeds the best human experts on almost every cognitive task is July 2032.
Dario Amodei put nine chances in ten on datacentre AI equal to a whole nation of top experts arriving within a decade, through a soft but steep takeoff.
Tamay Besiroglu places full replacement of remote workers by AI about five years ahead of Ege Erdil's date, which puts it near 2040.
Tom Davidson's takeoff model put a median of 2043 on AI able to readily automate all cognitive work, with about one chance in ten by 2030 and four in five by 2070.
Ege Erdil expects AI able to replace a remote worker at essentially every task to arrive around 2045.

Ajeya Cotra's biological anchors report modelled a median in the early 2050s for transformative AI, which she rounded to about 2050, with most aggressive and most conservative plausible medians of 2040 and 2080.
Holden Karnofsky gave better than one chance in ten of transformative AI by 2036, about even odds by 2060, and around two chances in three by 2100.
Joe Carlsmith gave about two chances in three that advanced, agentic, strategically aware AI becomes possible and affordable to build by 2070.
David Chalmers put his credence in human-level AI before 2100 at more than one half, while saying he would be surprised to see it within the next thirty years.

lanes.label: General or transformative AI

undated.line: Extrapolating past progress in AI subfields, Robin Hanson estimated that broadly human-level AI without brain emulation would take more than two to four centuries.
Gwern argued that once a scalable architecture exists, simply training ever bigger neural networks will keep yielding more sophisticated general abilities without fundamentally new designs.
Gary Marcus bet Miles Brundage that by the end of 2027 AI will still fail at least three of ten demanding tasks, from understanding films to Nobel-level discovery.
Yann LeCun says language models will not reach human-level intelligence, and that within five years we may at best know we are on the right path.

lanes.definition: AI far smarter than the best humans in every field, and how fast the step from human level to that would be.

forecasts.line: I. J. Good judged it more likely than not that a machine surpassing every human intellect would be built within the twentieth century, setting off an intelligence explosion.
The AI 2027 scenario has AI that automates AI research in early 2027 compounding into artificial superintelligence before that year is out.
Daniel Kokotajlo's August 2026 median for artificial superintelligence is March 2029, a few months after his median for AI that beats top experts.
Vernor Vinge expected humans to have the means to create superhuman intelligence within about three decades, and said he would be surprised if it came before 2005 or after 2030.
Leopold Aschenbrenner expected automated AI research to produce superintelligence, vastly smarter than people, before this decade is out.
Nick Bostrom clarified that, all things considered, he gave less than even odds that superintelligence would be developed by 2033.
Eli Lifland's August 2026 median for artificial superintelligence is July 2033, about a year after his median for AI that beats top experts.
The young Eliezer Yudkowsky cited 2035 as the most widely quoted date for the Singularity and said he, like many others, expected it substantially sooner.
Sam Altman wrote that superintelligence might arrive within a few thousand days, though it could take longer, and said he is confident it will come.
Ray Kurzweil set 2045 as the year of the Singularity, when machine intelligence created by people would vastly exceed all human intelligence combined.
Stuart Russell said superintelligent AI would probably arrive within his children's lifetimes, barring catastrophe, while calling it quite unlikely in the next few years.

lanes.label: Superintelligence

undated.line: Robin Hanson put less than one chance in a hundred on a single hand-coded AI leaping, without warning, from near impotence to overwhelming power.
Eliezer Yudkowsky argued that an AI improving itself would most likely either stall or take off explosively, since a gradual, human-paced takeoff would need implausibly precise diminishing returns.
Nick Bostrom judged it unlikely that the climb from human-level AI to superintelligence would take decades, and more likely that it would be fast or moderate.
François Chollet argued that an intelligence explosion cannot happen, and that the first superhuman AI would be just another step in steady, roughly linear progress.
Tom Davidson's best guess is that AI goes from matching human professionals at almost all cognitive work to far surpassing them in less than a year.
Paul Christiano put about one chance in seven on AI able to build a Dyson sphere by 2030, and about two chances in five by 2040.
Paul Christiano gave even odds on whether an intelligence explosion driven by software improvements alone is possible at all.
William MacAskill and Fin Moorhouse give roughly even odds that AI improving its own software sets off accelerating growth in AI capability.
Ege Erdil and Tamay Besiroglu doubt that AI improving its own software alone will set off an intelligence explosion, holding that compute and experiments bound progress.

lanes.definition: The economy growing far faster than it ever has, because machines can do the work that growth used to wait on.

forecasts.line: Robin Hanson cited his historical-trend projection, whose median put a switch to world output doubling every year or two at about 2025.

lanes.label: Explosive growth

undated.line: Robin Hanson's growth model implied that once machines can stand in for most human labour, world output would grow about ten times faster, doubling roughly every eighteen months.
Paul Christiano put about three chances in ten on a fast takeoff, expecting world output to finish a doubling over four years before any single-year doubling begins.
Tyler Cowen guesses AI will raise annual economic growth by only about half a percentage point, because slow-moving sectors such as government, health and education act as bottlenecks.
William MacAskill and Fin Moorhouse think it more likely than not that, once AI matches human researchers, a hundred years of technological progress follows in under a decade.
Tamay Besiroglu expects explosive economic growth, above thirty percent a year, once AI can flexibly stand in for human workers.

Experts surveyed by Ezra Karger and colleagues expect that if AI outperforms humans on many tasks by 2030, US growth would rise to around four percent a year, against about two and a half percent in their overall forecast.
undated.who: Ezra Karger and colleagues (Forecasting Research Institute)

undated.line: Phil Trammell argues that limits on splitting research across many AI workers could delay a technological singularity, though automating research would probably still produce an explosion.

lanes.definition: People losing control of the future to AI, either suddenly through a system that seizes it or slowly as human work, thought and consent stop mattering.

forecasts.line: Andrew Critch put about even odds, on top of other risks, on humanity gradually handing the planet to AI after it is built, mostly during the 2030s, with the last humans gone by 2050.

lanes.label: Loss of control

undated.line: Stephen Omohundro argued that any sufficiently advanced goal-seeking AI, unless deliberately designed otherwise, will resist being shut down, copy itself and acquire resources.
Paul Christiano expected that, without solving intent alignment, AI failure would come as a gradual loss of human steering to optimised proxies, possibly ending in a sudden cascade.
Toby Ord estimated about one chance in ten that unaligned AI causes an existential catastrophe within the next hundred years, the largest single risk he assessed.
Joe Carlsmith raised his estimate that power-seeking AI causes an existential catastrophe by 2070 from about one in twenty to more than one in ten.
Carl Shulman puts the chance that AI takes control of humanity's future at between a fifth and a quarter, depending on the day.
Jan Kulveit and co-authors argue that if AI keeps displacing human labour, thought and consent across economy, culture and state, humans will probably lose effective control without any takeover.
Daniel Kokotajlo puts his chance of catastrophe from AI at around seven in ten, a figure he calls infamously high.
Scott Alexander puts his chance of AI doom at about one in five, the lowest estimate among the authors of AI 2027.
Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nate Soares hold that if anyone builds artificial superintelligence with anything like today's methods and understanding, everyone on Earth will die.

lanes.definition: Machines that do useful physical work outside the lab, and factories that build more of them.

forecasts.line: Sam Altman said 2027 may bring robots able to carry out tasks in the real world.
The race ending of AI 2027 has special economic zones filling with robot factories from 2028, with a robot economy covering them by early 2030.
Hans Moravec expected machines to overtake people even in walking, manual dexterity and social skills within about fifty years of 1998.

lanes.label: Robots in the physical world

undated.line: Carl Shulman expects that once AI directs a converted industrial base, the robot population will double in under a year, and then within months.

lanes.definition: The computing, power and money the forecasts depend on, from revenue and investment to the size of the largest training clusters.

forecasts.line: Ray Kurzweil projected that around 2023 a thousand dollars of computer hardware would buy raw processing equal to his own estimate for one human brain.
The AI 2027 scenario forecast that during 2025 AI company revenues would triple, yearly data-centre spending would double, and US AI power draw would grow by over five gigawatts.
Daniel Kokotajlo foresaw that by 2026 AI assistants would be doing lucrative work across the economy, while world economic growth showed no visible acceleration yet.
Leopold Aschenbrenner expected single companies such as Google or Microsoft to reach AI revenue of around a hundred billion dollars a year by about 2026.
Leopold Aschenbrenner projected that total annual AI investment could exceed a trillion dollars by 2027.
Leopold Aschenbrenner projected that the largest training cluster would draw about ten gigawatts and cost hundreds of billions of dollars by 2028.
Hans Moravec projected that cheap computers would match the brain's processing power before 2030, bringing hardware suited to humanlike robots in the 2020s.
Ray Kurzweil forecast that before 2030 the combined thinking capacity of non-biological intelligence would exceed that of all human brains put together.
Leopold Aschenbrenner projected a trillion-dollar training cluster by 2030, drawing about a hundred gigawatts, more than a fifth of current US electricity output.
Yafah Edelman and Anson Ho of Epoch AI argue that longer data-centre build times push the first trillion-dollar AI compute cluster from about 2030 back to about 2035.

lanes.label: The build-out

lanes.definition: Copies of human minds running on computers, links between brains and machines, and medicine that outruns ageing.

forecasts.line: Ray Kurzweil expected robots the size of blood cells to be workable by around 2030, with scanning the living brain from the inside among their leading uses.
Ray Kurzweil expects the most diligent people to reach longevity escape velocity around 2030, gaining more than a year of life expectancy for every year that passes.
Ray Kurzweil predicts that during the 2030s nanobots will link the upper layers of the neocortex to the cloud, directly extending human thinking.

Anders Sandberg and Nick Bostrom concluded that, if electrophysiological-level models suffice, emulating a whole human brain should become feasible before 2050, with simple mammals ten to twenty years earlier.
Robin Hanson guessed that brain emulations would be the first machines able to replace human workers wholesale, arriving within about a century and then driving monthly economic doublings.

lanes.label: Minds, uploads and longer lives

undated.line: Robin Hanson argued that if brain uploads arrive before other human-level AI, cheap copying would multiply them and push wages toward subsistence even as total wealth grows.
Dario Amodei predicts that once powerful AI exists, biology and medicine will fit the coming half-century to century of progress into five to ten years.

questions.fast: Doubling at or faster than the pace the fastest scenarios assume.
questions.label: doubling time of the task length
questions.question: Does the length of task an AI can finish keep doubling as fast as the fastest forecasts need?
questions.slow: The doubling time stretching out, or the horizon stalling at a day or two of work.

questions.fast: Trials showing developers finishing work much faster with AI than without it.
questions.label: speed-up in the latest controlled trial
questions.question: Does AI speed up the people who build it, when that is tested in a controlled trial?
questions.slow: Trials showing little or no gain, as the first one did.

questions.fast: Independent tests showing agents doing more research work than the people overseeing them.
questions.label: a lab's own count of AI workdays per human workday
questions.question: Does any lab reach an AI that does the work of its own researchers?
questions.slow: The measure staying a lab's own claim, with no outside test.

questions.fast: The power drawn by the largest training runs keeps growing at its recent pace.
questions.label: doubling time of the power the largest training runs draw
questions.question: Does the power for the largest training runs actually get built?
questions.slow: The growth slowing as grid connections and turbines run short.

questions.fast: Spending staying high while the revenue it is meant to earn closes the gap.
questions.label: building and equipment spending against AI revenue
questions.question: Does the spending on computing survive, and does revenue catch up with it?
questions.slow: A cut in spending plans, or revenue falling further behind.

questions.fast: The gap staying short, so no single lab can pull away.
questions.label: months open models trail the best closed ones
questions.question: Do open and Chinese models stay only a few months behind the best closed ones?
questions.slow: The gap widening as the leading labs hold their best models back.

questions.fast: Few brakes, and releases that go ahead as soon as the models are ready.
questions.label: brakes the labs announced in the last year
questions.question: Do the labs keep pulling their own brakes, pausing a run or holding a model back?
questions.slow: More pauses and gated releases, of the kind a lab announces itself.

questions.fast: Hiring of young workers in exposed jobs falling well behind older workers.
questions.label: gap between young and older workers in exposed jobs
questions.question: Do young workers in the jobs most exposed to AI fall further behind?
questions.slow: The gap staying small, or closing.

questions.fast: Growth in output per person well above its long-run pace.
questions.label: output per person, change on a year
questions.question: Does output per person break away from its old growth rate?
questions.slow: Growth near its usual rate, year after year.

questions.fast: Robots doing everyday physical work outside factories, sold in large numbers.
questions.question: Do robots leave the lab and do useful physical work at scale?
questions.slow: Robots staying in demonstrations and controlled settings.

sources.work: Draft report on AI timelines (Biological Anchors)

sources.field: a former OpenAI researcher who leads the AI Futures Project and co-wrote the AI 2027 scenario
sources.finding: Daniel Kokotajlo foresaw that by 2026 AI assistants would be doing lucrative work across the economy, while world economic growth showed no visible acceleration yet.
sources.quote: The age of the AI assistant has finally dawned.

sources.field: an economics-trained AI researcher at Forethought who models AI takeoff speeds
sources.finding: Tom Davidson's takeoff model put a median of 2043 on AI able to readily automate all cognitive work, with about one chance in ten by 2030 and four in five by 2070.
sources.work: What a Compute-Centric Framework Says About Takeoff Speeds

sources.field: an AI alignment researcher who founded the Alignment Research Center and helped develop learning from human feedback
sources.finding: Paul Christiano put about one chance in seven on AI able to build a Dyson sphere by 2030, and about two chances in five by 2040.

sources.field: an AI alignment researcher who founded the Alignment Research Center and helped develop learning from human feedback
sources.finding: Paul Christiano put about three chances in ten on a fast takeoff, expecting world output to finish a doubling over four years before any single-year doubling begins.

sources.field: an AI alignment researcher who founded the Alignment Research Center and helped develop learning from human feedback
sources.finding: Paul Christiano expected that, without solving intent alignment, AI failure would come as a gradual loss of human steering to optimised proxies, possibly ending in a sudden cascade.
sources.quote: could cause a slow-rolling catastrophe

sources.field: a former OpenAI researcher and investor who wrote the Situational Awareness essays on AGI
sources.finding: Leopold Aschenbrenner expected single companies such as Google or Microsoft to reach AI revenue of around a hundred billion dollars a year by about 2026.

sources.field: a former OpenAI researcher and investor who wrote the Situational Awareness essays on AGI
sources.finding: Leopold Aschenbrenner called it strikingly plausible that models could do the job of the engineers and researchers who build AI by 2027.
sources.quote: by 2027, models will be able to do the work of an AI researcher/engineer

sources.field: a former OpenAI researcher and investor who wrote the Situational Awareness essays on AGI
sources.finding: Leopold Aschenbrenner expected automated AI research to produce superintelligence, vastly smarter than people, before this decade is out.
sources.quote: superintelligence by the end of the decade

sources.field: a former OpenAI researcher and investor who wrote the Situational Awareness essays on AGI
sources.finding: Leopold Aschenbrenner expects that in 2027 or 2028 models will be as capable as the leading experts and work much like a drop-in remote employee.
sources.work: Dwarkesh Podcast: Leopold Aschenbrenner, 2027 AGI and the return of history

sources.field: researchers at Epoch AI who study compute, data-centre build-outs and AI trends
sources.finding: Yafah Edelman and Anson Ho of Epoch AI argue that longer data-centre build times push the first trillion-dollar AI compute cluster from about 2030 back to about 2035.
sources.quote: longer lead times would delay this to around 2035
sources.work: Compute scaling will slow down due to increasing lead times

sources.field: the chief executive and co-founder of Anthropic
sources.finding: Dario Amodei put nine chances in ten on datacentre AI equal to a whole nation of top experts arriving within a decade, through a soft but steep takeoff.
sources.work: Dwarkesh Podcast: 'We are near the end of the exponential'

sources.field: the chief executive and co-founder of Anthropic
sources.finding: Dario Amodei predicts that once powerful AI exists, biology and medicine will fit the coming half-century to century of progress into five to ten years.

sources.field: the chief executive and co-founder of OpenAI
sources.finding: Sam Altman wrote that 2026 would likely bring AI systems able to work out genuinely new insights.
sources.quote: 2026 will likely see the arrival of systems that can figure out novel insights.

sources.field: the chief executive and co-founder of OpenAI
sources.finding: Sam Altman told TIME that OpenAI would have an internal system he would call AGI before the end of 2026, while conceding it was not there yet.

sources.field: the chief executive and co-founder of OpenAI
sources.finding: Sam Altman wrote that superintelligence might arrive within a few thousand days, though it could take longer, and said he is confident it will come.
sources.quote: It is possible that we will have superintelligence in a few thousand days

sources.field: a forecasting group led by Daniel Kokotajlo that wrote the AI 2027 scenario
sources.finding: The AI 2027 scenario has AI that automates AI research in early 2027 compounding into artificial superintelligence before that year is out.
sources.quote: leading to ASI by the end of 2027

sources.field: a forecasting group led by Daniel Kokotajlo that wrote the AI 2027 scenario
sources.finding: The race ending of AI 2027 has special economic zones filling with robot factories from 2028, with a robot economy covering them by early 2030.
sources.quote: By early 2030, the robot economy has filled up the old SEZs

sources.field: an AI forecaster, formerly at Open Philanthropy, who wrote the biological anchors report on AI timelines
sources.finding: Ajeya Cotra's median for the longest METR fifty-percent time horizon reported by the end of 2026 was about twenty-four hours of expert work.

sources.field: a philosopher and AI risk researcher who wrote a widely cited report on power-seeking AI
sources.finding: Joe Carlsmith raised his estimate that power-seeking AI causes an existential catastrophe by 2070 from about one in twenty to more than one in ten.
sources.work: Is Power-Seeking AI an Existential Risk?

sources.field: the chief executive and co-founder of Google DeepMind and a Nobel laureate in chemistry
sources.finding: Demis Hassabis expects AGI around 2030, give or take a year, and says that looking back people will see we are already on the lower slopes of the singularity.
sources.quote: we were standing in the foothills of the singularity now
sources.work: Demis Hassabis Thinks We're in the 'Foothills of the Singularity' (Stanford GSB)

sources.field: an economist at Epoch AI and Oxford who studies growth theory and AI-driven research
sources.finding: Phil Trammell argues that limits on splitting research across many AI workers could delay a technological singularity, though automating research would probably still produce an explosion.
sources.quote: Automating R&D will still probably produce a technological explosion
sources.work: Even after R&D is automated, parallelization constraints could delay a technological singularity

sources.field: a cognitive scientist and entrepreneur known as a leading sceptic of large language models
sources.finding: Gary Marcus bet Miles Brundage that by the end of 2027 AI will still fail at least three of ten demanding tasks, from understanding films to Nobel-level discovery.
sources.work: Where will AI be at the end of 2027? A bet (with Miles Brundage)

sources.field: a Turing Award-winning AI researcher who left Meta to found AMI Labs and works on world models
sources.finding: Yann LeCun says language models will not reach human-level intelligence, and that within five years we may at best know we are on the right path.

sources.field: an economist at George Mason University who writes Marginal Revolution
sources.finding: Tyler Cowen guesses AI will raise annual economic growth by only about half a percentage point, because slow-moving sectors such as government, health and education act as bottlenecks.
sources.quote: AI will boost economic growth rates by half a percentage point a year
sources.work: Why I think AI take-off is relatively slow (Marginal Revolution)

sources.field: researchers at the Forecasting Research Institute who survey experts and superforecasters on AI
sources.finding: Experts surveyed by Ezra Karger and colleagues expect that if AI outperforms humans on many tasks by 2030, US growth would rise to around four percent a year, against about two and a half percent in their overall forecast.
sources.who: Ezra Karger and colleagues (Forecasting Research Institute)
sources.work: Forecasting the Economic Effects of AI (NBER w35046)

sources.field: a statistician and Bletchley Park codebreaker who first described an intelligence explosion
sources.finding: I. J. Good judged it more likely than not that a machine surpassing every human intellect would be built within the twentieth century, setting off an intelligence explosion.
sources.work: Speculations Concerning the First Ultraintelligent Machine

sources.field: a mathematician who founded algorithmic probability and was an early pioneer of machine learning
sources.finding: Ray Solomonoff expected a general theory of AI most likely within two to twenty-five years, and a machine with human-level problem-solving in its designed fields perhaps as little as a decade or so later.
sources.work: The Time Scale of Artificial Intelligence

sources.field: a roboticist at Carnegie Mellon who compared computer power with the human brain
sources.finding: Hans Moravec projected that cheap computers would match the brain's processing power before 2030, bringing hardware suited to humanlike robots in the 2020s.
sources.work: When will computer hardware match the human brain?

sources.field: a co-founder of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute and a leading voice on AI extinction risk
sources.finding: The young Eliezer Yudkowsky cited 2035 as the most widely quoted date for the Singularity and said he, like many others, expected it substantially sooner.
sources.quote: 2035. Probably earlier.

sources.field: a philosopher who founded Oxford's Future of Humanity Institute and wrote Superintelligence
sources.finding: Nick Bostrom clarified that, all things considered, he gave less than even odds that superintelligence would be developed by 2033.

sources.field: researchers at Oxford's Future of Humanity Institute who studied whole brain emulation
sources.finding: Anders Sandberg and Nick Bostrom concluded that, if electrophysiological-level models suffice, emulating a whole human brain should become feasible before 2050, with simple mammals ten to twenty years earlier.

sources.field: a philosopher of mind at New York University known for work on consciousness
sources.finding: David Chalmers put his credence in human-level AI before 2100 at more than one half, while saying he would be surprised to see it within the next thirty years.

sources.field: an economist at George Mason University who studies long-run growth and brain emulations
sources.finding: Robin Hanson put less than one chance in a hundred on a single hand-coded AI leaping, without warning, from near impotence to overwhelming power.

sources.field: an economist at George Mason University who studies long-run growth and brain emulations
sources.finding: Robin Hanson's growth model implied that once machines can stand in for most human labour, world output would grow about ten times faster, doubling roughly every eighteen months.

sources.field: an economist at George Mason University who studies long-run growth and brain emulations
sources.finding: Robin Hanson argued that if brain uploads arrive before other human-level AI, cheap copying would multiply them and push wages toward subsistence even as total wealth grows.
sources.quote: uploads would reproduce quickly, and wages would fall

sources.field: an economist at George Mason University who studies long-run growth and brain emulations
sources.finding: Robin Hanson guessed that brain emulations would be the first machines able to replace human workers wholesale, arriving within about a century and then driving monthly economic doublings.
sources.work: The Age of Em: Work, Love, and Life when Robots Rule the Earth

sources.field: a computer scientist who described the basic drives of goal-seeking AI
sources.finding: Stephen Omohundro argued that any sufficiently advanced goal-seeking AI, unless deliberately designed otherwise, will resist being shut down, copy itself and acquire resources.
sources.quote: Without special precautions, it will resist being turned off

sources.field: an AI researcher who created the Keras library and the ARC benchmark for general intelligence
sources.finding: François Chollet argued that an intelligence explosion cannot happen, and that the first superhuman AI would be just another step in steady, roughly linear progress.
sources.quote: I argue that intelligence explosion is impossible

sources.field: a pseudonymous independent researcher and writer known for early arguments about AI scaling
sources.finding: Gwern argued that once a scalable architecture exists, simply training ever bigger neural networks will keep yielding more sophisticated general abilities without fundamentally new designs.
sources.quote: we can simply train ever larger NNs and ever more sophisticated behavior will emerge

sources.field: a philosopher who founded Oxford's Future of Humanity Institute and wrote Superintelligence
sources.finding: Nick Bostrom judged it unlikely that the climb from human-level AI to superintelligence would take decades, and more likely that it would be fast or moderate.

sources.field: a computer scientist at Berkeley who co-wrote the standard AI textbook and studies AI control
sources.finding: Stuart Russell said superintelligent AI would probably arrive within his children's lifetimes, barring catastrophe, while calling it quite unlikely in the next few years.
sources.work: Human Compatible: AI and the Problem of Control

sources.field: a philosopher at Oxford who studies existential risk
sources.finding: Toby Ord estimated about one chance in ten that unaligned AI causes an existential catastrophe within the next hundred years, the largest single risk he assessed.
sources.work: The Precipice: Existential Risk and the Future of Humanity

sources.field: a co-founder of DeepMind who now leads Microsoft AI
sources.finding: Mustafa Suleyman predicted an AI could turn a modest stake into a million dollars selling online, with light human help within a year and probably entirely on its own within three to five years.

sources.field: an independent researcher who studies the economics and strategy of advanced AI
sources.finding: Carl Shulman puts the chance that AI takes control of humanity's future at between a fifth and a quarter, depending on the day.
sources.quote: depending on the day I might say one in four or one in five

sources.field: an independent researcher who studies the economics and strategy of advanced AI
sources.finding: Carl Shulman expects that once AI directs a converted industrial base, the robot population will double in under a year, and then within months.
sources.quote: robot doubling time that is less than a year

sources.field: a former OpenAI researcher who leads the AI Futures Project and co-wrote the AI 2027 scenario
sources.finding: Daniel Kokotajlo puts his chance of catastrophe from AI at around seven in ten, a figure he calls infamously high.
sources.work: Dwarkesh Podcast: AI 2027 with Scott Alexander and Daniel Kokotajlo

sources.field: a researcher who co-founded Mechanize after work at Epoch AI on AI economics
sources.finding: Ege Erdil expects AI able to replace a remote worker at essentially every task to arrive around 2045.
sources.quote: Maybe for me, that would be around 2045.
sources.work: Dwarkesh Podcast: AGI is still 30 years away (Ege Erdil and Tamay Besiroglu)

sources.field: the founder and the president of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute
sources.finding: Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nate Soares hold that if anyone builds artificial superintelligence with anything like today's methods and understanding, everyone on Earth will die.
sources.work: If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies

worlds.label: A managed explosion
worlds.text: Superintelligence arrives within a few years and the economy grows faster than ever, but governments and labs slow down enough to keep the systems checked.

worlds.label: A long diffusion
worlds.text: AI keeps improving but spreads at the pace of earlier technologies, growth rises without exploding, and the disruption falls on particular jobs and places.

worlds.label: Control slips away
worlds.text: Either a race produces systems nobody can check, or people are slowly made irrelevant as AI takes over the work, thought and choices that gave them a say.

worlds.label: The brake
worlds.text: Progress slows, either because people choose to stop it or because capability, power or money runs out first.
